newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serb court condemned over murder trial.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb court condemned over murder trial.

text.p: A Bosnian Serb court drew international condemnation on Tuesday after concluding a murder trial against Moslem men who were denied the right to choose their defence lawyers.
"By any stretch of the imagination this could not be considered a fair trial," Simon Haselock, a spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, told Reuters.
The four men charged with murder face possible death sentences. The Serb court is scheduled to announce a verdict in the case on Thursday.
The Serb court, ignoring protests from human rights groups, has refused to allow the defendants to be represented by lawyers from Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and assigned them lawyers.
The defence lawyers were permitted only about five minutes to present their case on Tuesday, Haselock said.
The murder trial in the eastern town of Zvornik ended on the second day of proceedings after only 34 minutes of direct testimony.
Three of seven Moslem defendants are charged with murdering four Serb woodcutters, another is charged with killing a Moslem and all seven are charged with illegal possession of firearms.
The office of the High Representative and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said Bosnian Serb authorities had denied the accused basic legal rights.
"This is a kangaroo court," David Foley, a spokesman for the OSCE said. "They didn't even pay attention to the proper form of a trial."
The "Zvornik seven" surrendered voluntarily to NATO peacekeeping troops last year in Serb-controlled territory and U.S. troops handed them over to Serb authorities.
U.N. officials later said Serb police obtained confessions from the defendants after beating them.
The men were found near the former Moslem enclave of Srebrenica, the site of a massacre of Moslem men by conquering Bosnian Serb forces in July 1995.
Up to 8,000 Moslem men are still missing from Srebrenica, believed executed or gunned down as they tried to flee the enclave.
The Serbs have labelled the defendants as "terrorists". Federation authorities say the men were hiding in the hills since the fall of Srebrenica.
Haselock warned that international aid to Bosnian Serb territory was linked to compliance with the Dayton peace treaty and respect for international legal standards.
"It shouldn't be a surprise why so little aid money is going to Republika Srpska (Serb republic) when its institutions act in such a fashion," Haselock said.

Under the peace agreement which ended the Yugoslav conflict in November 1995, Bosnian authorities are obliged to abide by the European Convention on Human Rights which guarantees defendants the right to freely choose their own counsel.
